prompt: In the shop's app, which function decides that `charge` runs after `reserve_stock` and before `ship`?

choices.text: `start_order`, because it passes the order in
choices.why: The client function starts the instance and answers; it says nothing about the steps.

choices.text: `order_flow`, the orchestrator
choices.why: Yes: the order of its `yield`s is the order of the steps.

choices.text: `reserve_stock`, by returning before the others
choices.why: An activity does one step and never knows what comes after it.

choices.text: The extension bundle, from the order of the functions in the file
choices.why: The bundle carries the extension; the order of the steps is in the code.

prompt: On the laptop the first order was answered with HTTP 500, and the host's log blamed the webhooks. What was missing?
hint: The log line named a setting.

choices.text: The package `azure-functions-durable` in the image
choices.why: It was installed; without it the file would not have loaded and the host would have found no functions.

choices.text: A key, because the route asks for `FUNCTION` level
choices.why: `DFApp` was given `ANONYMOUS`, so the route asks for no key.

choices.text: `WEBSITE_HOSTNAME`, a setting Azure gives every app it runs
choices.why: Yes: the client needs it to write the status addresses, and a container on a laptop has to be given it.

choices.text: The History table, which Azurite only creates on the first order
choices.why: The task hub's tables are the extension's business, and their absence is not what the log named.

prompt: Match each part of the shop's Durable Functions app with what it does.
hint: One description belongs to nothing in this lesson.

pairs.right: starts an instance and answers with its addresses
says which steps run, and in what order
does one step of the work
holds the state of every instance of the app

right_distractors: turns the decorators into a `function.json` per function

prompt: The shop uses the order number as the instance id. Which of these are true on this host? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A second start for an order still `Pending` is refused
choices.why: Yes: the second POST for A-1002 got a 500 saying the instance already exists.

choices.text: A start for an order that has completed runs it again from the beginning
choices.why: Yes: `NonRunningStates` may be started over, and A-1002 ran a second time.

choices.text: The id makes the activities safe to run twice
choices.why: It guards only while the instance runs; activities still have to be written to be repeated.

choices.text: Two instances in the task hub can share an id if their inputs differ
choices.why: An id is unique within the task hub whatever the input.

choices.text: The status address carries the id in its path
choices.why: Yes: `.../instances/A-1001?...`.

prompt: The client function answered 202 at once, and its ___ header carried the address to poll, with `Retry-After` beside it.
hint: An HTTP header that says where something is.

prompt: An orchestrator calls five activities one after another, each with its own `yield`, and then returns. How many times does the orchestrator function run for one instance?
With the two clocks in the log line, `now` changed on every run for A-1003 and `context` did not. Why?

choices.text: It is read from the history, so a replay gets the first run's time
choices.why: Yes, and that is what makes it safe to decide anything from.

choices.text: `context` is the time the container started
choices.why: The container had been up for a while; the value was the time of the first run of A-1003.

choices.text: `datetime.now()` is cached by the worker between runs
choices.why: It is the one that moved; nothing cached it.

choices.text: The orchestrator ran only once and logged four lines
choices.why: Four runs: the first had `replaying=False` and the other three `True`.

prompt: The shop wants a random discount code for each order, chosen inside the orchestration and used in a later step. Where should the code be made?

choices.text: In the orchestrator, with `random.choice` seeded by `datetime.now()`
choices.why: A seed from the clock differs on every replay, so every replay picks a different code.

choices.text: In the orchestrator, with `uuid.uuid4()`
choices.why: A new value on every replay; the documentation points to `context.new_guid()` instead.

choices.text: In an activity, whose result the history keeps
choices.why: Yes: replays read the stored result instead of running it again.

choices.text: In an environment variable the orchestrator reads
choices.why: One value for every order, and one that can change between replays.

prompt: Put in order the four rows the first run of `order_flow` added to A-1001's history.
trap: Putting `ExecutionStarted` first: every run, the first included, opens with `OrchestratorStarted`.

prompt: A team wants to move a running app's task hub from the Azure Storage provider to the Durable Task Scheduler. What does the documentation say?

choices.text: Data cannot be migrated between providers: create a new app on the new provider
choices.why: Yes, in a note on the providers page.

choices.text: Change `storageProvider` in `host.json` and the instances move on the next start
choices.why: The setting chooses a backend for new state; nothing copies the old one across.

choices.text: Export the History table and import it into the scheduler's dashboard
choices.why: No such import exists; the dashboard shows the scheduler's own instances.

choices.text: Rewrite the orchestrators, because the scheduler needs a different API
choices.why: The documentation says existing apps use the scheduler with no code changes.

prompt: What in `order_flow` made the six reservations of A-1005 run at the same time?

choices.text: One `yield` on `task_all` over tasks made without `yield`
choices.why: Yes: the tasks are scheduled together in one checkpoint and awaited once.

choices.text: A thread per line, which `task_all` starts behind the scenes
choices.why: No thread anywhere: the activities run in the host, not in the orchestrator.

choices.text: Declaring the orchestrator with `async def`
choices.why: Forbidden: a Python orchestrator is a generator.

choices.text: A setting in `host.json` that runs activities in parallel
choices.why: The file was lesson 15's, unchanged; the code alone did it.

prompt: An order of 100 lines runs on one host with 4 processors and the default of 10 activities per processor. Each `reserve_line` takes 1 second. Ignoring the time between activities, how many seconds at least do the reservations take?
On a plan that has added a second instance of the app, where can the activities of one fan-out run?

choices.text: Only on the instance that holds the orchestrator's control queue
choices.why: That is the orchestrator; activities are stateless.

choices.text: On either instance, since both compete for the work-item queue
choices.why: Yes, which is how a fan-out uses the instances a plan adds.

choices.text: On whichever instance received the HTTP request
choices.why: The request only started the instance; the work goes through the queue.

choices.text: On a third instance kept for activities
choices.why: There is no such instance; every instance of the app runs both kinds.

prompt: One of the six `reserve_line` calls of an order raises an exception. What does the documentation say happens to `yield context.task_all(tasks)`?

choices.text: It returns five results, with `None` in place of the one that failed
choices.why: It does not return partial results.

choices.text: It retries the failed call by itself until it succeeds
choices.why: Retries happen only with `call_activity_with_retry` and a `RetryOptions`.

choices.text: It fails at the first error, which `try` and `except` catch
choices.why: Yes; uncaught, the instance ends `Failed`.

choices.text: The other five are cancelled and their stock released
choices.why: Nothing undoes their work; any compensation is the orchestrator's to write.

prompt: A nightly job fans out to 20,000 items in one orchestration, and every replay has become slow. Which are among the documentation's answers? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Split the work into sub-orchestrations, each with its own history
choices.why: Yes: each child replays only its own rows.

choices.text: Have activities return a reference to a blob rather than the data
choices.why: Yes: what an activity returns is stored and read back on every replay.

choices.text: Raise `partitionCount` to 64
choices.why: Sixteen is the most, and partitions do not shorten a history.

choices.text: Run the loop over the items in a thread inside the orchestrator
choices.why: An orchestrator may do no work and no input or output of its own.

prompt: Suppose `order_flow` left out `timeout.cancel()`. A-1007 is paid one second into its ten-minute window. What does its status say a minute later?

choices.text: `Completed`, because the payment won the race
choices.why: The documentation says an instance is not marked `Completed` while a timer it created is pending.

choices.text: `Failed`, because a timer was left behind
choices.why: Leaving one is not an error; it only delays the end.

choices.text: `expired`, because the timer fires later
choices.why: `task_any` already returned the payment; the branch for the timer never runs.

choices.text: `Running`, until the timer fires
choices.why: Yes, which is why the code cancels the loser.

prompt: The payment for A-1009 was raised after the customer's cancellation had terminated it. What did the management API answer?

choices.text: 202 Accepted, and the event was kept for later
choices.why: A buffered event is for an instance that will still wait; this one had finished.

choices.text: 404 Not Found
choices.why: The instance exists, terminated; 404 is for an id the hub does not have.

choices.text: 410 Gone
choices.why: Yes: the documentation's answer for an instance that has completed or failed.

choices.text: 400 Bad Request, because the body was not JSON
choices.why: The body was JSON with a JSON content type.

prompt: A-1011 waited for payment, a new version of the code was deployed, and the payment then made it fail. What did the failure compare?

choices.text: The new image's id with the id of the image that started the instance
choices.why: Nothing compares images; the restart with the same image worked.

choices.text: The step the new code asked for with the one in the history
choices.why: Yes: a timer in the history, an activity in the replay.

choices.text: The host id, which a new container would change if it were not fixed
choices.why: It was fixed with `AzureFunctionsWebHost__hostid`, which is why the address still worked.

choices.text: The event's body with the input that `charge` expects to receive
choices.why: The code never reached `charge`; the replay failed before it.

prompt: In Python a single durable timer can last at most ___ days, so a longer wait is a loop of shorter timers.
A webhook from the bank sometimes delivers the same payment confirmation twice. With the event raised for each delivery, what must hold?

choices.text: Nothing: the extension drops the second event because the names match
choices.why: The documentation says events are delivered at least once, duplicates included.

choices.text: The orchestrator must use `async def` to await only the first
choices.why: An orchestrator is never a coroutine.

choices.text: Handling a confirmation must be safe to repeat
choices.why: Yes: the documentation recommends exactly that for at-least-once delivery.

choices.text: The bank must be given the terminate address instead
choices.why: Terminating ends the instance; it is not a way to pay.

prompt: Put in order what a client sees when it starts an order and follows the asynchronous HTTP pattern to the end.
items: Polling `Location` answers 202 while the instance runs
Polling `Location` answers 200 when the instance has finished
The body of that answer carries `output`
trap: Expecting the output in the first answer: the client function returns before any step has run.

prompt: Instances of `order_flow` are waiting for payments. Which of these changes is breaking for them?

choices.text: Changing the text of the log line at the top of the orchestrator
choices.why: A log line is not a request; replays make the same calls.

choices.text: Making `ship` sleep two seconds instead of one
choices.why: Inside an activity, and activities have no replay.

choices.text: Adding an unrelated HTTP function to the app
choices.why: It changes no orchestrator.

choices.text: Calling a new activity before the wait for payment
choices.why: Yes: exactly what made A-1011 fail.

prompt: A-1010 was waiting when the container restarted, and the payment raised afterwards completed it. What carried it across the restart?

choices.text: The Python worker, which kept the generator paused in memory
choices.why: The worker was restarted with the container; nothing in memory survived.

choices.text: Docker, which saves a container's processes on restart
choices.why: `docker restart` stops the processes and starts them again from nothing.

choices.text: The instance's row and history in the task hub, which the new host read
choices.why: Yes: the state was in Azurite all along.

choices.text: The timer, which was paused for the length of the restart
choices.why: A timer is a message with a time on it; it does not pause.
